details:
AstroTerrain – Project Description

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

AstroTerrain is an AI-powered planetary terrain analog exploration platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It aims to explore and identify Earth locations that share measurable terrain and environmental characteristics with selected regions on the Moon and Mars.

The platform brings together planetary datasets, Earth-based geospatial information, feature comparison, similarity scoring, and interactive 3D visualization. Users can select a planetary target and explore potential terrestrial analog locations through the platform.

AstroTerrain follows a modular architecture consisting of four major components:

  • Frontend: Provides an interactive exploration interface, planetary target selection, Earth globe visualization, candidate markers, and comparison dashboards.
  • Backend: Uses FastAPI and PostgreSQL with PostGIS to manage target information, spatial records, analog-search requests, and geospatial processing.
  • ML Engine: Provides preprocessing, missing-value handling, topographical, climatic and geochemical comparison, candidate ranking, explainability, and report-generation modules.
  • Scientific Data Pipeline: Organizes real datasets from Earth, lunar, and Martian missions and sources, including Copernicus, NASA POWER, LOLA, Diviner, MOLA, CRISM, and THEMIS.

The system compares available features and calculates similarity scores based on configurable weights. It also considers data availability and feature coverage so that missing measurements are not incorrectly treated as matching values.

2. What benefits does the project provide?

AstroTerrain provides a unified environment for exploring planetary and terrestrial datasets. Its key benefits include:

  • Makes planetary terrain comparisons easier to explore through a single interface.
  • Brings together scientific datasets from multiple Earth-observation and planetary missions.
  • Supports data-driven comparison of topographical, climatic, and geochemical characteristics.
  • Provides explainable comparison results and feature-availability information.
  • Encourages the reuse and exploration of existing scientific datasets.
  • Offers a modular architecture that can be expanded with additional datasets, algorithms, and visualization capabilities.

3. What is the intended impact?

The long-term goal of AstroTerrain is to support planetary analog research and make scientific exploration more accessible. Earth-based analog environments can help researchers, students, and mission planners investigate terrain and environmental conditions relevant to planetary exploration.

By connecting Earth observations with lunar and Martian datasets, AstroTerrain aims to encourage interdisciplinary research involving planetary science, geospatial technology, machine learning, and remote sensing.

It can also serve as an educational and research-oriented platform for understanding how Earth-observation technologies contribute to space exploration.

4. What technologies and tools were used?

The project was developed using the following technologies:

Programming languages

  • Python
  • JavaScript
  • TypeScript
  • SQL
  • HTML and CSS

Frontend and visualization

  • React.js
  • Vite
  • Three.js

Backend and database

  • FastAPI
  • PostgreSQL
  • PostGIS
  • SQLAlchemy
  • Pydantic

Machine learning and geospatial processing

  • Python-based ML and feature-comparison modules
  • NumPy
  • Rasterio
  • GeoPandas
  • Shapely
  • PyProj

Development and infrastructure

  • Docker and Docker Compose
  • Git and GitHub
  • Git LFS
  • Visual Studio Code
  • NASA and other scientific data repositories

The project primarily uses software-based tools and publicly available scientific datasets. No specialized hardware was required for the prototype.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

AstroTerrain combines planetary science, Earth observation, geospatial analysis, and machine learning into one modular exploration platform.

Its creative aspect lies in treating Earth as a source of potential analog environments for other planetary bodies. Instead of examining lunar and Martian terrain in isolation, the platform explores how measurable characteristics can be compared with terrestrial locations.
